transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-21
Start: 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Samira Khan (Redwood SE), Dr Emily Chen (CTO - Orchid Imaging), Marcus Li (Head IT), Tara Gomez (Compliance)

Summary:
Orchid Imaging is evaluating a hermetic/private on-prem Redwood deployment for clinical imaging workloads. Key concerns: offline/air-gapped update process, hardware constraints (single-rack GPU density and limited NVMe), FIPS/HSM integration, auditability, and acceptable latency/cost trade-offs. They want a pilot to validate throughput and a formal security review before procurement.

Topics covered:
- Current infra and constraints (rack, NIC, internet egress policy)
- Offline upgrade process & signed images for air-gapped sites
- Hardware footprint and quantization tradeoffs for latency
- Security controls: SSO, SAML, KMS/HSM, FIPS, audit logs
- Timeline for pilot and gating criteria

Quick action-items captured in call: see metadata.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, we'll run quick intros. I'm Jordan, AE on the Redwood Private team, with Samira, our SE.
[00:10] Dr Emily: Hi it's Emily here, CTO at Orchid. Marcus and Tara are with me.
[00:15] Marcus: Marcus. Hi.
[00:17] Tara: Tara, compliance. Thanks.
[00:20] Samira: Awesome. Quick agenda — understand your constraints, sketch recommended topology, and outline an air-gap update process. Sound good?
[00:28] Dr Emily: Yes. We have pretty strict controls. No egress from our inference cluster, so any updates need to come via signed offline bundle or have to be manually applied.
[00:36] Jordan: Got it. So fully hermetic. Two immediate questions — what's your hardware footprint and what's your throughput target?
[00:44] Marcus: We're currently planning for a single rack, about 4 GPUs that are A100-ish. To be realistic we've got limited NVMe per node, and the data plane is isolated behind a jump host. We also need to keep PII logs offsite, so minimal retention.
[00:58] Samira: Ok. That helps. For single-rack setups we typically recommend either Redwood Dedicated or Redwood Private deployed in VPC-less mode with our air-gapped update tooling. The tradeoff is batch size vs latency — with 4 GPUs you'll get decent throughput but tail latency can matter for live reads.
[01:20] Tara: From compliance — any update mechanism must be verifiable: signed artifacts, SHA hashes, and audit log entries. We require FIPS-compatible crypto and prefer HSM-backed keys.
[01:33] Jordan: Absolutely — we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key wrapping, and our image signing supports FIPS 140-2 compatible keys. Slight note — sometimes the term 'Key Managament' gets mangled in transcripts, but yes, we mean KMS.
[01:45] Dr Emily: How do you handle KV cache or long context for our imaging models — we have big KV needs, is that a problem on limited NVMe?
[01:55] Samira: Good point. We call it KV cache — sometimes transcript says 'KV cash' — but practically, our runtime keeps state in RAM with spill-to-disk when needed. On limited NVMe we recommend tuning the KV eviction policy, plus model quantization to reduce memory. We can run numbers for your typical sequences.
[02:17] Marcus: On quantization — we had been worrying about 4-bit lower-quality outputs. Does Redwood support quantized kernels that still preserve diagnostic quality?
[02:28] Samira: Yes — we have validated 8-bit and 4-bit paths for several open models and provide quality monitors. For clinical workloads, we typically run a small eval suite to validate. We'll propose a rolling canary: start with 8-bit in pilot, compare metrics, then consider 4-bit with regen tests.
[02:45] Tara: And about access control — we need SAML SSO, role-based access, and audit logs for every API call. Can you ensure no plaintext tokens are stored off-site?
[02:56] Jordan: Yes. Our private deployment supports SAML/SSO and RBAC. Tokens are short-lived and audit logs can be kept locally; we also have an option to ship a read-only log bundle out via secure courier if that's permitted.
[03:10] Dr Emily: Courier? So you mean physically exporting logs?
[03:13] Jordan: Yeah, some customers prefer signed log bundles on an encrypted USB for compliance reviews — it's not ideal but it's an option for hermetic environments.
[03:22] Marcus: Ok. For updates, our security policy says maintenance windows must be scheduled quarterly and a security person must be present for image flashing. 
[03:30] Samira: That's aligned with our typical air-gap workflow — we prepare a signed update artifact, an operator follows a checklist to apply, the node verifies signature using HSM-backed key, then we run post-upgrade smoke tests. All steps are logged.
[03:44] Tara: Do you support code signing with our HSM or do you require Redwood's key?
[03:49] Samira: We can do customer-managed keys; the signing process can be performed by your HSM. If you prefer Redwood to sign, we provide an audit trail; but in high-regulated setups we usually recommend customer signing.
[04:00] Dr Emily: One worry — latency. Our inference calls are often part of a clinical workflow, 95th percentile latency target is < 200 ms for small image prompts. Is that realistic on your stack?
[04:11] Samira: On a single rack of A100s, for smaller context sizes and optimized kernels we can hit sub-200ms for many models, but it depends on model size and quantization. If you need deterministic p95, Dedicated with pinned capacity reduces variability. We can instrument your workload in a pilot.
[04:28] Marcus: What about CPU and NIC requirements — we have 25GbE and older CPU nodes; will that choke batching?
[04:36] Samira: 25GbE is generally OK for modest QPS, but for heavy batching or multi-GPU KV sync we recommend 100GbE. Older CPUs are fine for I/O, but if you plan heavy pre/post-processing on the same host, that can be a bottleneck. We can give a reference baseline.
[04:51] Jordan: Also note, we can offer a hybrid route — keep sensitive logic on prem and call a hosted Redwood route for non-sensitive embeddings or non-PHI tasks, that reduces load and cost. But I understand Orchid wants everything hermetic for now.
[05:05] Dr Emily: For pilot scope — what would you need?
[05:08] Jordan: Ideally: a representative prompt set (anonymized), access to rack inventory, and your acceptance criteria — p95 latency, throughput, and quality thresholds. Pilot duration we typically plan 6–12 weeks for hermetic runs.
[05:22] Tara: We won't share PHI sample data. We can provide synthetically generated prompts that mimic distribution.
[05:27] Samira: That's perfect — synthetic sets work for perf and regression checking. For quality checks we sometimes run a small blinded clinician evaluation with a subset of prompts.
[05:36] Marcus: On maintenance — do you provide a way to patch the inference engine without full reboot? Our uptime target is 99.9% during hours.
[05:44] Samira: We have warm restart and rolling update paths; though in fully hermetic small clusters rolling updates can be limited by capacity. If you want no downtime, you need at least N+1 capacity.
[05:55] Dr Emily: Can you do on-disk dedupe and image compression? Storage is tight.
[05:59] Samira: We have cache compaction and recommend model sharding strategies to reduce disk footprint. We'll include expected NVMe needs in our hardware checklist.
[06:10] Jordan: Any procurement or security process milestones we should know?
[06:13] Tara: We'll need SOC 2 Type II, ISO27001 summary, penetration test report, and a supply chain attestation. Also ATO-ish paperwork for internal review.
[06:23] Jordan: We can share SOC2 and prior penetration test summaries; supply chain attestation might take a bit but we'll surface what we have.
[06:29] Dr Emily: Cost — how do you price private deployments? Is it a flat license, or per-GPU plus support?
[06:36] Jordan: For Private deployments it's usually a platform fee + capacity-based license (per-GPU or per-inference unit) and optional support tiers. For dedicated on-prem we can structure reserved capacity pricing. We'll send a pricing sketch after the pilot scope is defined.
[06:50] Marcus: Are there known integrations for HSM vendors? We run Thales and a YubiHSM in some branches.
[06:58] Samira: We have integrations with common HSM vendors; YubiHSM and Thales are in our tested list. We'll note exact firmware requirements in the checklist.
[07:08] Tara: Any concerns about data exfil? Auditing needs to be very granular.
[07:12] Jordan: We support per-request audit logs, and logs can be stored locally. For exfil controls, we can disable outbound telemetry; the only outbound artifacts would be operator-initiated bundles.
[07:23] Dr Emily: On the technical deep-dive side — can you do a stress-run with our synthetic set and show how latency behaves with batch sizes?
[07:30] Samira: Yes — for the pilot we can run a synthetic benchmark and provide a spreadsheet with p50/p90/p95 across batching and quant configs.
[07:39] Marcus: Also want to understand rollback — if an update causes regressions, how do you revert in an air-gap?
[07:43] Samira: We keep prior images signed and tested; rollback is a documented procedure and also signed. We recommend keeping at least two validated images on site.
[07:53] Jordan: Quick note on competitive positioning — some customers looked at LambdaLabs for on-prem hosting but they lacked a formal air-gap update flow and strong SOC documentation. Anthropic private options were discussed as well, but pricing and integration risk came up.
[08:08] Tara: Ok. Timeline constraints — procurement wants vendor selection by end of year. Pilot ideally in Q1 '27.
[08:15] Jordan: That lines up. If we can get checklist and perf numbers by end of Oct, we can propose pilot in Jan.
[08:22] Dr Emily: Do you have any template for the operator runbook we can review?
[08:26] Samira: Yes, we'll attach an operator runbook template showing update steps, smoke tests, and rollbacks.
[08:33] Marcus: For telemetry — you said it's optional. If we enable minimal telemetry for health, can it be pushed over our private management VLAN to a logging host?
[08:41] Samira: Absolutely — we can ship logs to a customer-managed syslog endpoint; nothing needs to leave the cluster unless you export a bundle.
[08:48] Tara: One more compliance Q — do you support per-tenant encryption keys? We need separation between clinical units.
[08:55] Samira: We support tenant-level keying and per-route encryption. We'll map out how that looks in the architecture doc.
[09:02] Dr Emily: Great. Any other blockers?
[09:05] Jordan: Just to confirm, Marcus will send rack/network details, Tara will confirm the allowed maintenance windows, and we'll follow up with the checklist and pilot scope.
[09:14] Marcus: Yep. I'll pull configs and reach out.
[09:16] Tara: I'll coordinate with legal on ATO items.
[09:19] Jordan: Perfect. We'll aim to get the SOC and architecture slides to you by Sunday, and Samira will run perf estimates.
[09:28] Dr Emily: Quick practical: for the signed artifact — what format? ISO image, tarball?
[09:33] Samira: Typically a signed tar.gz with detached signature; for large images we provide a signed ISO. We'll include checksum and a verification script.
[09:41] Marcus: How do we run smoke tests without internet? Are tests included in the bundle?
[09:46] Samira: Yes, smoke tests are part of the update artifact; after install they run locally and emit a test report which you can keep.
[09:53] Tara: Cool. That addresses most compliance concerns.
[09:56] Jordan: Ok final recap — next steps: Jordan share SOC2 and private-deploy doc, Samira run perf table, Marcus/Tara provide infra & windows, schedule on-site follow-up. Any objections?
[10:09] Dr Emily: No objections. Looks good.
[10:12] Marcus: Sounds good.
[10:14] Tara: Thanks, speak soon.
[10:16] Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email with links and proposed dates.

End transcript.
